'''''Quercus castaneifolia''''', the '''chestnut-leaved oak''', is a species of [[oak]] in the turkey oak section [[Quercus sect. Cerris|''Quercus'' sect. ''Cerris'']]. It is native to the [[Caucasus]] and [[Alborz]] mountains of [[Iran]], and resembles the closely related [[Quercus cerris|Turkey Oak]] in appearance.

==Description==
''Q. castaneifolia'' is a [[deciduous]] [[tree]] growing up to {{Convert|35|m|abbr=off}} tall, with a trunk up to {{Convert|2.5|m|ft|abbr=on|frac=2}} in diameter (exceptionally up to 50 m tall with a trunk up to 3.5 m across).<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.nativetreesociety.org/worldtrees/europe/europe2005/european_trees.htm | title = European Trees | publisher = [[Eastern Native Tree Society]] | access-date = 2008-11-25 | archive-date = 2008-11-22 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20081122001212/http://www.nativetreesociety.org/worldtrees/europe/europe2005/european_trees.htm | url-status = dead }}</ref> The [[leaves]] are {{Convert|10–20|cm|abbr=off|frac=2}} long and 3–5 cm wide, with 10–15 small, regular triangular lobes on each side. The [[flower]]s are wind-pollinated [[catkin]]s; the [[fruit]] is an [[acorn]], maturing about 18 months after pollination, 2–3 cm long and 1.5–2 cm broad, bicoloured with an orange basal half grading to a green-brown tip; the acorn cup is 2 cm deep, densely covered in soft {{Convert|4–8|mm|abbr=off|frac=8}} long 'mossy' bristles. The acorns are very bitter, but are eaten by [[jay]]s and [[pigeon]]s; [[squirrel]]s usually only eat them when other food sources have been exhausted.{{citation needed|date=June 2016}}

==Cultivation==
The tree was introduced to England in 1846, but remains relatively rare in collections despite being a vigorous grower. A tree from the original introduction is at the [[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]],<ref>{{cite web |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:295924-1 |title=Kew: Plants: Chestnut-leaved Oak, Quercus castaneifolia |publisher=www.kew.org |access-date=2016-05-11 }}</ref> another survives at the [[Harlow Carr]] arboretum in [[Yorkshire]].{{Cn|date=September 2025}}

The [[cultivar]] ''Quercus castaneifolia'' 'Green Spire' has been selected for its erect growth.{{Cn|date=September 2025}}

==Notable specimens==
A specimen of ''Quercus castaneifolia'' found in the Hyrcanian forest of northern Iran on 29. April 2021 by Alireza Naqinezhad is considered to be the tallest oak in the world.
It has a height of 60.4m, a diameter of 4.9m, and a circumference of 22m.
The finding was published in a tweet by Pieter De Frenne, professor of forestry at the faculty of Bioscience Engineering at Ghent University.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://twitter.com/PieterDeFrenne/status/1388213327856377856 |title=Pieter De Frenne on Twitter |publisher=www.twitter.com |access-date=2021-05-22 }}</ref>
